title: Inference and Margin of Error, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: Inference means using a sample to say something about a whole population. A sample is a small group that was actually measured, and the population is the larger group we care about.
The SAT asks you to scale a sample result up to a population estimate, to read and compare margins of error and confidence intervals, and to judge which sampling method gives trustworthy results.
Most of these questions need careful reading more than calculation, so we will focus on what each phrase means.
A random sample represents the population it was drawn from. That is what lets us scale the sample results up to the whole population.
beats.item: A random sample represents its population

beats.say: To estimate a count in the population, multiply the sample proportion by the population size.
A sample result is an estimate. The margin of error gives a range of plausible values, which is the estimate plus or minus the margin of error.
Larger random samples give smaller margins of error. But sample size does not fix bias. A large biased sample is still biased.
beats.item: Bigger samples help, but do not fix bias

beats.say: If two intervals overlap, the data do not clearly show which population value is larger. If they do not overlap, there is convincing evidence of a difference.
The population estimate equals the count in the sample, divided by the sample size, multiplied by the population size. The fraction is the sample proportion.
To estimate how many do not have a trait, use the complement. Either subtract the estimate from the population, or use one minus the sample proportion.

card.text: Not having the trait: use the complement

scenes.title: Estimates and intervals
rows: interval from E − M to E + M

beats.say: If you know the estimate and the margin of error, the interval runs from the estimate minus the margin, to the estimate plus the margin.
If you know the interval, the estimate is the midpoint, the average of the two endpoints.
And the margin of error is half the width of the interval, which is the upper endpoint minus the lower endpoint, divided by two.
Easy example. An inspector tests a random sample of two hundred fifty phones from a shipment of fifteen thousand, and finds nine defective. Estimate the number of defective phones in the shipment.

card.sub: Shipment of 15,000. Estimate the defective count.

beats.say: First find the sample proportion, the fraction of the sample that was defective. Nine out of two hundred fifty.
Nine divided by two hundred fifty is zero point zero three six. So three point six percent of the sample was defective.
Because the sample was random, we assume the whole shipment has about the same fraction of defective phones. So we multiply the proportion by the shipment size.
Zero point zero three six times fifteen thousand is five hundred forty. So we estimate that about five hundred forty phones in the shipment are defective.
As a check, set up a proportion. Defective phones over phones tested equals the unknown over the shipment size.
Cross-multiply, which means multiplying diagonally. Two hundred fifty times x equals nine times fifteen thousand.
Fifteen thousand divided by two hundred fifty is sixty, and nine times sixty is five hundred forty. So x equals five hundred forty, which matches.
To recap. A random sample lets us scale up. Multiply the sample proportion by the population size to get an estimate.
An interval is the estimate plus or minus the margin of error. Overlapping intervals show no clear difference.
